title: Restrictive Digital Regulations Could Cut Indian Startup Formation by 20 Percent, Oxford Economics Warns
excerpt: A new report projects a 25% decline in venture capital flows and 245,000 fewer startup jobs by 2035 if India tightens its digital regulatory framework.
body:
• An Oxford Economics report warns that restrictive digital regulations could cut Indian startup formation by 20%, eliminating approximately 2,130 new startups annually through 2035
  • Venture capital investment could fall 25%, representing an annual loss of approximately ₹91,500 crore, while 245,000 fewer startup jobs would be supported by 2035
  • The report surveyed 550 ecosystem participants including 350 startups, 100 VC firms, and 100 incubators across India
  • An enabling regulatory approach could instead boost startup formation by 7% and increase VC investment by 9%

The Numbers Paint a Stark Picture

A comprehensive new report by Oxford Economics, commissioned by Digital Prosperity Asia, projects that a shift toward more restrictive digital regulations in India could reduce annual startup formation by 20% — the equivalent of roughly 2,130 fewer companies launching each year between 2026 and 2035.

The economic modelling goes further. Venture capital flows could shrink by 25%, wiping approximately ₹91,500 crore from annual investment. By 2035, the report estimates 245,000 fewer jobs would be supported in India's startup ecosystem compared to the current trajectory — losses concentrated in technology hubs like Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Delhi-NCR.

What the Ecosystem Is Saying

The findings draw on a survey of 550 participants across India's startup landscape — 350 startups, 100 venture capital firms, and 100 incubators — combined with expert interviews and quantitative economic modelling. The picture that emerges is one of an ecosystem under strain.

"Venture capital flows could shrink by 25%, wiping approximately ₹91,500 crore from annual investment."

Eighty-eight percent of startups surveyed said digital regulations impose operational constraints. Nearly three-quarters of startups and VC firms reported that resources are being diverted from research and innovation toward compliance activities. And 68% of startups said digital regulations have increased uncertainty around future returns.

"The regulations could impede the growth of technology-driven enterprises."

— Mohandas Pai, former CFO of Infosys

Mohandas Pai, former Infosys CFO and a prominent voice in India's venture capital community, has publicly called for a review of the pending digital rules. His concerns were echoed by startup founders at a roundtable organized by the Confederation of Indian Industry in New Delhi.

What's Driving the Regulatory Squeeze

The regulations under discussion span data governance, cross-border data flows, and compliance requirements for digital platforms. Key measures include the Personal Data Protection Bill, amendments to the Information Technology Act, and new guidelines on content moderation and foreign direct investment in digital platforms.

The government frames these measures as essential for data security and consumer protection, with officials emphasizing a phased two-year implementation and provisions for SME exemptions. But the report's analysis suggests the combined effect of stricter compliance costs and restricted access to international data services could diminish India's attractiveness as a launchpad for technology-driven ventures.

Venture capital firms including Sequoia Capital India and Accel Partners have expressed concern in a joint letter to the Finance Ministry, citing the study's projections as evidence of potential capital flight.

The Flip Side: An Enabling Path

The report also models a more optimistic scenario. An even more enabling regulatory approach — emphasizing risk-based and proportionate regulation, global regulatory interoperability, and regulatory sandboxes for AI — could boost startup formation by 7%, increase VC investment by 9%, and support an additional 80,000 startup jobs by 2035.

The report highlights three principles for strengthening the ecosystem: risk-based regulation particularly for emerging technologies like AI, greater interoperability with global regulatory frameworks, and clearer guidance to reduce compliance uncertainty for early-stage companies.

Why It Matters for NRIs

India's startup ecosystem is deeply intertwined with its diaspora. Many of India's most successful startups were co-founded by NRIs or received their earliest funding from diaspora investors. A regulatory environment that slows formation and shrinks capital flows has direct implications for NRIs who invest in, advise, or plan to return to build companies in India. The report's findings add urgency to a debate that will shape whether India can sustain its position as the world's third-largest startup ecosystem.
